observation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems can handle simple dialogue tasks, but complex tasks remain difficult because naively chaining LLMs induces cascading hallucinations and logic inconsistencies. Real-world LLM agent frameworks tend to oversimplify the complexities of collaborative problem solving and often rely on unstructured natural-language dialogue, which loses information across rounds and produces unproductive chatter. Existing code-generation methods also lack self-correction mechanisms that verify runtime executability, leaving complex software engineering tasks unmet.

claims: LLM-based agents have advanced automatic-programming development.
ReAct and Reflexion use chain-of-thought prompts to generate reasoning trajectories and action plans with LLMs.
The two approaches demonstrate that a ReAct-style loop of reasoning is effective for empowering automatic programming.
ToolFormer and ToolLLM can learn to use external tools through simple APIs.
One role-play framework for programming involves communication between agents playing different roles.
Another framework utilizes multiple agents for software development.

The role-play and multi-agent software-development frameworks have not fully exploited effective workflows with structured output formats, which makes it harder to deal with complex software engineering issues.
The broader meta-programming line of work has also included code models such as CodeBERT and recent projects such as CodeLlama and WizardCoder.

claims: LLM-based agent systems tend to oversimplify the complexities of real-world applications.
They struggle with effective, coherent, and accurate problem solving when collaborative interaction is important.
Many LLM-based multi-agent works improve problem-solving abilities by integrating discussions among multiple agents.
Stable-Alignment builds instruction datasets from consensus on value judgments reached by LLM agents in a sandbox.
Some works on LLM agents focus on sociological phenomena, such as Generative Agents, which creates a town of 25 agents.
NL-SOM uses agents with different functions interacting through multiple rounds of mindstorms to solve complex tasks.
A cost-reduction model combines large language models as tool makers with small language models as tool users.
Some LLM multi-agent works address cooperation and competition in planning and strategy and propose LLM-based economies, focusing on open-world human behavior simulation.
LLM-based agents face pitfalls such as assistant repeated instruction and infinite loops of messages.
These pitfalls become more urgent in task-oriented collaborations that require consistent and mutually beneficial interactions.

claims: Public code benchmarks such as HumanEval and MBPP contain function-level code tasks, unlike datasets that focus on real-world software engineering aspects.
On a seven-task SoftwareDev comparison, AutoGPT, LangChain, and AgentVerse obtain an average executability score of 1.0, failing to produce executable code, while ChatDev obtains 2.1.

In the statistical analysis on SoftwareDev, ChatDev has an executability of 2.25, consumes 19,292 tokens, generates 1.9 code files, 77.5 total code lines, 40.8 lines per code file, requires 762 seconds, and has a human revision cost of 2.5.
AgentVerse, like general-purpose agent frameworks, lacks the ability to systematically deconstruct requirements for complex software systems.

solution.idea: The core insight is to transfer mature human organizational practices, namely Standard Operating Procedures, into LLM-based multi-agent collaboration. Instead of letting agents engage in free-form dialogue, each agent plays a specialized role in a simulated software company and produces standardized intermediate artifacts such as product requirement documents, system designs, interface definitions, task lists, code, and test code. These structured handovers reduce ambiguity and information loss, prevent irrelevant chat and cascading hallucinations, and make complex software engineering tasks tractable by decomposing them into a role-specific assembly line. The approach also uses a shared publish-subscribe message pool to make communication efficient and an executable feedback loop to correct runtime errors, targeting the key failure of prior methods that lacked runtime self-correction.
solution.implementation: MetaGPT defines a simulated software company with specialized roles: Product Manager, Architect, Project Manager, Engineer, and QA Engineer. Each agent profile contains name, profile, goal, constraints, role-specific context, and skills; all agents operate in a ReAct-style loop in which they observe relevant messages from the shared environment and then trigger actions. Work follows a Standard Operating Procedure: first, on receiving user requirements, the Product Manager performs analysis and produces a structured Product Requirements Document containing Original Requirements, Product Goals, User Stories, Competitive Analysis, Requirement Analysis, and Requirement Pool. Next, the Architect converts the PRD into a system design that includes an implementation approach, Python package name, file list, data structures, interface definitions, and sequence flow or program call diagrams. Then the Project Manager decomposes the design into a task list, treating each code file as a separate task and assigning it to Engineers. Engineers write the actual code, execute it, and refer to the PRD, system design documents, previous messages, and code files when debugging. Afterwards, the QA Engineer generates unit tests and reviews the code to fix bugs and ensure quality. The final structured assembly is output as a complete software solution. Communication is structured rather than natural-language chat: each role publishes documents and diagrams to a shared global message pool, and agents subscribe to messages relevant to their role profiles; an agent activates its action only after all prerequisite dependencies are available, avoiding one-to-one requests and information overload. Executable feedback is integrated as follows: after initial code generation, the Engineer writes and runs unit tests; if tests fail, the Engineer inspects stored messages, compares the code with the PRD and system design, debugs the code, and reruns tests iteratively until the tests pass or a maximum of three retries is reached.
